description: Our team is a group of friends who have built projects together before, including hackathons, and we work well because we share all our ideas and always execute them correctly. We bring a mix of computer science, engineering, biology, and physics, so we like tackling problems that sit between the subjects.
summary:
FlameWatch is a fire-safety dashboard for crewed habitats on the Moon and in orbit. NASA recommends Moon base air with 34% oxygen at 8.2 psi, much richer than the 21% on the ISS, and in that air fires start more easily and spread faster. NASA has studied fire in space for decades, but the results are split across 24 separate experiments in its PSI database, each in a different format.

We combined all 24 into one table of 2,186 test runs. You pick a habitat (Moon base, ISS, pressurized rover or spacesuit) and FlameWatch shows a 0-100 fire-risk score, the NASA experiments that tested air closest to yours, and a chart of conditions nobody has tested. An SI assistant answers questions using NASA's data and names its source. Our ESP32 sensor box feeds live smoke, heat, crew and hatch readings into the dashboard and closes a vent when a fire starts.

This matters because the evidence runs out exactly where it's needed: only 32 of 1,738 NASA test runs come close to Moon base air. FlameWatch helps engineers/researchers check their designs against real data and shows NASA what to test next.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

FlameWatch answers a simple question for anyone designing or living in a space habitat: how risky is a fire in this air, and what has NASA actually tested under these conditions and what can they find out about it?

You start by picking a habitat: a Moon base at NASA's recommended 34% oxygen and 8.2 psi, the ISS at 21% and 14.7 psi, a pressurized rover, or a spacesuit at pure oxygen. The dashboard then shows:

- A fire-risk score from 0 to 100, built from four parts: oxygen-rich air, smoke, heat and flame. Each part is shown separately with a one-line explanation, so nobody has to trust a black box.

- The 24 NASA PSI combustion experiments, ranked by how many of their test runs were close to your habitat's air. Click any experiment to see what it burned, what it measured and what it found, or compare up to three side by side.

- A chart of every NASA test run by oxygen and pressure, with a box around your habitat. For a Moon base, only 32 of 1,738 runs fall inside it, and none of those burned the fabrics or plastics a cabin is made of.

- An SI assistant (Claude) that answers questions like "Which materials are riskiest at this oxygen level?" from NASA's data, and names the experiment behind each answer.

- A 3D model of each habitat. Pressing "Simulate a fire" plays a 30-second fire: smoke fills the module, the vent closes, the alarm goes off, the crew leave, the hatch seals and CO2 puts it out. The spacesuit gets its own script, because a suit has no vent and nowhere to go.

HOW IT WORKS

A Python script downloads all 24 combustion investigations through PSI's public API. Every experiment stores its data differently, so a cleaning script matches up column names, converts units, and splits cells that hold several values. It also leaves out rows that would mislead: summary rows that only give ranges, and burner gas that isn't cabin air. The result is one table of 2,186 test runs, each still linked to its NASA file and row.

A run counts as "close" to your habitat if it's within 4 points of oxygen and 30% of the pressure. The FastAPI backend does the matching, ranking and scoring, and the frontend draws everything in plain JavaScript with Three.js and Chart.js.

PSI has no lunar-gravity fire data yet, so we added three NASA studies: in lunar gravity Mylar kept burning at 15.6% oxygen (21.2% on Earth), acrylic flames spread at 1.5 mm/s instead of 4.0, and NASA suggests an oxygen safety margin of up to 2.3 points for materials used on the Moon. Flames spread slower there but survive at lower oxygen, so Earth's standard flammability test may not be strict enough for a Moon base.

THE SENSOR BOX

Our hardware is a prototype of early-warning equipment for a habitat module. An ESP32 reads a smoke input, a temperature sensor, a motion sensor (is the crew inside?), an ultrasonic sensor (is the hatch closed?) and a dial that sets the oxygen level. It posts readings every second, and the server replies with what to do. LEDs show green, yellow or red, the buzzer sounds on a warning, and a servo closes the vent on smoke or a sudden heat rise, because in low gravity airflow is what feeds a fire. The heat trigger gets more sensitive as oxygen goes up. If someone is still in the module, it tells them to evacuate before suppression starts.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Habitat engineers can check a cabin's air against NASA evidence before a design is locked in. NASA researchers can see exactly which conditions have never been tested and plan the next experiment. Anyone building a fire model can download the matching test runs as a CSV. The same physics applies on Earth wherever air is enriched with oxygen, such as hospital oxygen therapy and hyperbaric chambers.

It covers all three goals of the challenge: habitat relevance (presets and a live risk score), data for predictive modeling (one clean dataset and CSV export) and next-generation safety equipment (the sensor box).

TOOLS

Software: Python, FastAPI, JavaScript, HTML/CSS, Three.js, Chart.js, Anthropic's Claude API(Sonnet 5.5). Hosting: Render (backend) and GitHub Pages (frontend). Hardware: ESP32 programmed in Arduino C++, temperature, motion and ultrasonic sensors, potentiometers, LEDs, a buzzer and a servo.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Most tools would show NASA's data as a jumbled list. We connected it to a habitat you can see, set on fire and watch respond, and tied it to real hardware that reacts the way a habitat system would. We also didn't stop at what PSI covers: the chart shows where NASA's data runs out, and the lunar studies fill in what's known
